subtopic: RETURN OF RUSSIAN JEWS FROM UNITED STATES.
speechtext:
The attention of the Department of the Interior was called to the announcement that fifty Russian Jews had been returned from Fargo, North Dakota, to Winnipeg by the United States authorities. An inquiry was at once sent to the Commissioner of Immigration at Winnipeg, and he replied by telegraph on the 24th instant that the only people deported from Fargo, as charged, consisted of one Russian Jew family-father, mother and four children- who lived in Winnipeg for four years, and went to the United States a year ago. Nothing further is known of the family referred to.

ROSS (Ontario)-by Mr. Calvert -asked :
1.	Is the cotton plant grown for commercial purposes in Canada ?
2.	Have any experiments ever been made by the government on any of its experimental farms, or at other points in Canada, to determine whether cotton could be profitably grown ?
If so, what were the results ?

1.	No.
2.	From 1890 to 1893 some experiments were made in the growing of cotton at the Central Experimental Farm. Seed of some of the earlier varieties was obtained for the purpose and sown in plots. The seed germinated and the plants grew, and before winter set in they also bloomed, but the frost cut them before any cotton formed. These experiments were repeated for several years with the same results. Cotton plants have been grown in the green-house at the Central Experimental Farm and cotton produced, but no success has attended the efforts to raise cotton in the open air. No experiments with cotton have been conducted at any of the other experimental farms, as the average mean temperature for the growing period is higher at Ottawa than it is at any of the branch experimental farms. The department is not aware that experiments in the growing of cotton have been made at any other points in Canada.

speakeroldname: Mr. F. D. MONK (Jacques Cartier) moved:
speechtext:
That the Dominion government, having a controlling interest in the Montreal Turnpike Road Trust, should enter into negotiations without delay with the provincial government of Quebec, that has jurisdiction over said trust, with the view of obtaining the abolition of the present system of toll-gates existing on the island of Montreal.
He said : By this motion I desire to call the attention of the government and the House to a reform which is very desirable, and which though it may be local in its scope, interests a very large number of people in the district of Montreal. The toll-gate system in the neighbourhood of Montreal is replete with so many abuses, that it behooves this government as well as the government of the province of Quebec, to address themselves towards remedying the evil which exists. The turnpike toll system in the neighbourhood of Montreal is a system which has become thoroughly obsolete, and which does not obtain, I believe, in other parts of Canada or in the United States. That farmers, and gardeners, and people generally who have dealings with the city of Montreal can only enter the city by paying toll. It is true these tolls are not excessive ; it is true that under the present system of administration they are necessary in order to obtain sufficient funds to keep the roads in a thorough state of repair. Be that as it may, the system is antiquated and the toll-gate has become a worn out institution. So far as I know, the old-fashioned system of toll-gates lias been abolished everywhere in the United States, and I think I am safe in saying that they do not exist in the vicinity "of Toronto. People who drive around the mountain of Montreal and who come from other parts of the country, are surprised that we have not long ago abolished the toll-gate system. That system, such as we have it in Montreal, has been established a long time. In fact, I think the legislation which governs the present Turnpike Trust dates from before the establishment of responsible government in our province. The subject of reforming that system has very often been discussed at public meetings and in the public press, and is under discussion at the present time throughout the island of Montreal and even beyond. I have taken some interest in this question since I entered parliament. because it interests the county or Jacques Cartier to no inconsiderable extenr. Previous to the existence of this parliament

I have myself. On the trust itself, there are men like Mr. Galibert, the president of the trust, who is well versed in matters of this kind. Mr. Thos. Trenholine, of Montreal West, has given that matter special study and will certainly be competent to propose some solution to the government. Mr. Richard White was, for several years, president of the trust and has much practical knowledge of the subject and there are no doubt other men whose names could be suggested to the government who could without much expense and within a very short space of time lay before the government an improved scheme for the administration of the roads upon the island of Montreal tending to the immediate abolition of toll-gates, and the safeguarding and the giving of more popular character to the interests concerned, giving to the administration a stronger representation and giving general satisfaction throughout the city of Montreal and the counties interested. I have no doubt that could be done by a commission of one or of three appointed upon an understanding between this government and the government of Quebec, and could be done in a short space of time and at very little expense. I might mention for the information of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that several years ago there was a question of the abolu-tion of the toll-gates. The matter was discussed by the turnpike trustees themselves, and X have been informed that at one time the city of Montreal was disposed to pay one-quarter of any sum that would be required to keep the high roads upon the island of Montreal in good order. I think, myself, that the negotiations might very properly be renewed between the trust and the city of Montreal, or at any rate, the possibility of the city sharing an even larger proportion of the expense necessary for the maintenance of these roads might be looked into by the commission of inquiry X have just suggested to my hon. friend, because I believe that it is in the interest of the city of Montreal to pay more than one-quarter ol' the sum required. I believe that the city of Montreal is more capable of contributing towards that expense, naturally, than all the other municipalities, and I believe it has also more interest in doing so. It hi in the interest of the city of Montreal that the roads, the important avenues in the vicinity of the city should be kept in first-class order, should be pleasant and agreeable to drive upon and should be at all times available without any tolls to people coming in from the country as well as to visitors and Montrealers themselves driving into the country. The farmer, the milkman and the gardener, as my hon. friend knows, must recoup themselves for the tolls which they are called upon to pay from their customers, and the carters, who in large numbers drive out from the city of Montreal, do not, as far as my experience goes, pay these tolls to oblige their fares, but they take them out

I hardly think that my hon. friend (Mr. Prfifontaine) who has just taken his seat has fully understood the object I have in view. No doubt, any municipality in the county could say : We will take the road and keep it in repair, and abolish the toll-gates. But they would have to pay $4,000 a mile for the road-

If my hon. friend will allow me-they will have to pay $4,000 a mile for the road if they wish to be relieved of paying the . interest. But that is not what has happened. The municipalities have assumed that the road has cost $4,000 a mile, and they have assumed to keep it in order and pay the interest at the rate of 4 per cent on $4,000 a mile. That is what they undertook to do twenty-five years ago.

I think the hon. gentleman has forgotten that it is stated in the return that ' on the following roads the municipalities paid 6 per cent on the value of the road, say $4,000 a mile and keep up the roads.
That is exactly what I say.

In Hochelaga they pay $262. 73. This arrangement may be made in such municipalities as Hochelaga and St. Louis de Mile-End, but where would the money come from to maintain the long roads outside the city ?
The municipalities there -would do the same thing.

But the municipality of St. Laurent would have eight or ten miles of road to keep in order for the people of Montreal but would receive no money from Montreal for the maintenance of the road. My hon. friend sees that that would be eminently unfair.

I wish to put a question to my hon. friend. Does the city of Montreal receive anything from those who pass on the roads, the taxes on which are commuted roads in such municipalities as Ste. Cunegonde, St. Henri, St. Louis de Mile-End and Maisonneuve ? They pay nothing.

They pay taxes in the city of Montreal. But my hon. friend must see that there is no proportion between a municipality like Montreal with a valuation of $200,000,000 and St. Laurent with a valuation of $800,000. The idea is that, as everybody or. tiie island used the roads, there should be a system of contribution by which everybody would pay.

If my hon. friend will allow me, I think that the municipali-



ties that have acceded to this arrangement have a population of certainly three-quarters of the whole island of Montreal.

But the arrangement does not work, for, as my hon. friend knows, it gives rise to a great deal of difficulty. I have received a letter dated 25th of March, from the corporation of Westmount by its secretary, which says, in part:
There are about two miles in length of the road of the trustees of the Montreal Turnpike Roads situated in Westmount on which the tolls were commuted some years ago, since which, time the trustees have done nothing to maintain the road though they object to sell it to the town alleging want of authority to alienate.
X do not wish to pursue this further ; but my bon. friend will see that, with the system he suggests, the poor people would pay for the rich, and the moment a piece of road is handed over to the municipality the trustees lose control of it. It is well enough in the municipalities in the neighbourhood of Montreal. But when you come to a long piece of road outside the city it is not reasonable to throw the maintenance exclusively on the municipality, as in Lachine and St. Laurent. The people of Montreal use these x'oads more than the farmers, and if you abolish toll-gates you -would have no revenue. The roads would have to be maintained by the municipality without any fund to draw upon for their maintenance. I would like to say one word to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), who has asked me to abandon this resolution. He says that the Department of Finance and this government has no control whatever over that body called the Montreal Turnpike Trust. Does he remember that the Dominion names three trustees and that the policy of the body is, therefore, under the absolute control of the Minister of Finance ?

I have listened with great attention to the remarks made upon this subject by my hon. friend from Jacques earlier (Mr. Monk) ; but I am sorry to say that after having listened to him once, twice, or three times this afternoon. I still fail to know exactly what he wants, and

The right hon. gentleman did not know what he wanted, and he has only found out lately.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: My hon friend from Jacques Cartier has pointed out the evils from which he thinks the people on the island of Montreal are suffering. Upon that we are all agreed. He has pointed out that the system which now prevails for obtaining access from the island to the city is obsolete, out of date, antiquated. Upon that we are all agreed also. But, he has not pointed out the remedy which he thinks should be applied. He says : You are the creditors and you ought to do something. But the government tells him : We have no jurisdiction in this matter, we are simply the creditors, we have advanced money and we have not received any interest upon It. We are quite ready to modify the preseut arrangement if a satisfactory proposal is made. I would ask my hon. friend what he thinks ought to be done. My hon. friend the Minister of Marine and Fisheries (Mr. Pre-l'ontaine) has suggested that perhaps a good basis for settlement would be the adoption of the arrangement which was made some twenty, years ago when other municipalities similariy situated-the municipalities of Mai-sonneuve and Hochelaga-made a settlement which was the natural one to adopt; that is to say the municipalities interested hi these roads and which are traversed by them should assume the jurisdiction and care of these roads as all municipalities do.
And stand all the expense alone ?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: That is another question. But here is the difficulty which justifies the amendment of my hon. friend the Minister of Inland Revenue (Hon. Mr. Brodeur). My hon. friend from Jacques Cartier objects to the municipalities taking over the roads. His reasons may be good or bad, I do not know. I do not examine them at the present time. But it strikes me, and I suppose the friends of my hon. friend would agree with me, that the most natural method by which to achieve a settlement of this question would be that all the municipalities interested and which are crossed by these roads should assume jurisdiction over them and do as municipalities generally do-become responsible for the maintenance of them. But my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier does not want the question to be settled in this way. Then, what is the method by which he wants to have it settled ? He has spoken for about two hours, but he has failed to tell us what he wants. He points out the grievance, but

And now we are asked to give away the balance of the investment, because this motion invites us to go to the provincial government with a view of abolishing the toll-gates on the island of Montreal. We are asked to abolish the toll-gates which, provide the source of revenue from which the people of Canada may expect some day to be paid, in part at least, for their investment. That is the plain proposition as it is put to us, and it is for this House to say whether or not it will accept it. I have a toll-gate system in my county, and why should I not have the benefit of such a proposition as well as my hon. friend from Jacques Cartier ? The hon. member for Levis (Mr. Demers) has the toll-gate system in his county, and why should he not have the benefit of It also ? Where is this going to lead us to ? I do not believe they have. They have been relieved of the obligation to maintain the roads all this time, and it seems to me it would be unfair to the people of other parts of the country if these gentlemen were now relieved of the obligation to pay any toll or rent whatever for the money which has gone into the construction of these roads.
But, independent of that, we have absolutely no jurisdiction to deal with this matter. The provincial legislature alone can absolutely and exclusively determine the conditions under which these people are to be relieved. It was decided by the Privy Council in the case of Belleau and the Queen, that the provincial legislature has exclusive jurisdiction in these matters.
The motion asks you to enter into negotiations with the provincial government.

speechtext: That is not what the motion proposes.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: There is the province which is the mortgagor who owns the property, and there is the party of the second part, the people who live in the district and benefit by the roads, and who are obliged to pay the tolls ? That is a sensible way to go about it, but there is no sense in coming to this parliament in the first instance. It seems to me, that is an elementary principle. The only relief my hon. friend (Mr. Monk) can get here is to have us abandon our clainr to these bonds, so as a result his constituents may be relieved of the obligation to pay these tolls.
